policies.title: Work with missing or stale data
policies.decision_question: Can the coach make a useful decision when one or more expected inputs are absent?
trigger: A planned daily or weekly decision is due and an expected Garmin, derived, or subjective field is null, stale, or implausible.
suggested_action: Do not infer that a missing observation is normal.
Use the most recent trustworthy plan and symptom information to offer a conservative proceed/modify choice.
State which missing field limits confidence and ask one blocking clarification only when safety or session classification cannot otherwise be resolved.
alternatives: Use a lower-impact or shorter alternative that preserves the plan intent.
Defer optimization while keeping the agreed run frequency unchanged.
do_not_apply_when: A medical red flag is present; use clinical escalation policy instead.
policies.rationale: No readiness algorithm is reliable enough to require every wearable field. Transparent handling of missingness is safer than silent imputation.
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate staleness windows to each field and the import cadence.
policies.uncertainty: The best conservative fallback depends on the planned session and the missing field.
review_triggers: Missing symptom data before a demanding session

policies.title: Do not overreact to one poor night
policies.decision_question: Should one suboptimal night of sleep change today’s training?
trigger: One night is worse than the athlete’s usual sleep or the consumer sleep score is low, while illness, tendon symptoms, and perceived fatigue are normal and recent recovery has otherwise been stable.
suggested_action: For an easy or routine session, generally proceed and reduce ambition rather than cancel automatically.
For a demanding session, retain an easy fallback and decide from warm-up response, coordination, effort, and symptoms.
Record the observation for trend review.
alternatives: Shorten duration
Remove optional fast elements
Swap with the nearest easy session without adding a make-up session
do_not_apply_when: Several poor-recovery days have accumulated.
Illness, unusual fatigue, coordination problems, worsening pain, or clinician restrictions are present.
policies.rationale: Severe sleep loss impairs performance on average, but evidence is weaker for one ordinary poor night; consumer sleep scores are noisy.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for severe sleep loss; low for a single ordinary night
policies.athlete_applicability: High, because the desired coaching behavior is adherence without ignoring deterioration
policies.threshold_basis: Trend- and symptom-based heuristic; no universal score cutoff
policies.calibration_needed: Learn the athlete’s response to isolated poor nights and distinguish bedtime duration from device stage estimates.
policies.uncertainty: An apparently normal subjective state can still miss impairment; use warm-up response and avoid maximal testing.
review_triggers: Pain worsens during or after training

policies.title: Escalate accumulated recovery deterioration
policies.decision_question: Should training be reduced when several recovery signals worsen together?
trigger: Multiple consecutive days show worsening fatigue, sleep, resting physiology, soreness, mood, or performance, especially when subjective and objective signals agree.
suggested_action: Modify the next demanding exposure first rather than rewriting the entire plan from one score.
Favor easy running, rest, or low-impact aerobic work according to symptoms and the athlete’s preference.
Investigate illness, accumulated training, life stress, and fueling as competing explanations.
alternatives: Keep duration but remove intensity when mechanical tolerance is good
Keep frequency but reduce session size
Take a rest day when systemic symptoms or marked fatigue make training unproductive
do_not_apply_when: The pattern is explained by a known transient factor and the athlete feels normal during a controlled warm-up; still document uncertainty.
policies.rationale: Readiness evidence favors combining subjective and objective signals; HRV-guided superiority is inconsistent and protocols differ from Garmin scores.
policies.threshold_basis: Individual trend heuristic; no universal HRV/RHR/readiness cutoff
policies.calibration_needed: Establish the athlete’s own normal ranges and define “consecutive” only after enough clean data.
policies.uncertainty: Fatigue has many causes and the dashboard cannot diagnose them.
review_triggers: Fever, chest pain, fainting, unusual breathlessness, or systemic illness appears

policies.title: Stage return after respiratory illness
policies.decision_question: How should running resume after an illness interruption?
trigger: Recent acute respiratory illness has interrupted training and symptoms are now very mild or resolved without cardiopulmonary or systemic red flags.
suggested_action: Begin with a controlled, easy exercise challenge rather than restoring the prior quality or long run immediately.
Monitor during, immediately after, and through the following day before progressing.
Rebuild session duration and demanding work in stages; do not make up missed sessions.
alternatives: Walk-run or shorter easy run
Low-impact aerobic work
Additional rest when symptoms are not clearly improving
do_not_apply_when: Chest pain, syncope, palpitations, unusual dyspnea, fever/systemic illness, or clinician restriction is present.
The illness was moderate/severe or involved complications; obtain appropriate clinical guidance.
policies.rationale: IOC guidance supports a symptom-led exercise challenge in selected mild cases, while cohort data distinguish first training from full training and full performance.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate clinical guidance; low-moderate cohort evidence
policies.athlete_applicability: High for uncomplicated respiratory illness; lower for any uncharacterized illness
policies.threshold_basis: Consensus-supported exercise challenge; exact progression requires calibration
policies.calibration_needed: The IOC example of 10–20 minutes around 60–70% of normal intensity is a consensus example, not an automatic prescription.
policies.uncertainty: Illness type and severity are unknown unless supplied; return-to-performance timelines vary widely.
review_triggers: Symptoms recur during or after challenge

policies.title: Symptoms outrank favorable Garmin scores
policies.decision_question: Can a favorable readiness score justify training through worsening tendon symptoms?
trigger: PTT-region symptoms are worse, function is reduced, or the delayed response is deteriorating even though Garmin readiness, HRV, sleep, or load metrics look favorable.
suggested_action: Let the symptom/function trend drive modification.
Avoid using a proprietary composite score as clearance for the planned run.
Choose rest, a lower-impact alternative, or a reduced run only within previously tolerated bounds and any clinician guidance.
alternatives: Preserve upper-body or otherwise nonprovocative strength work
Use low-impact aerobic work if tolerated
Seek clinical assessment when the pattern is progressive or unclear
do_not_apply_when: The symptom report is stale or refers to a different body region; clarify first.
policies.rationale: Wearable readiness has no validated injury-clearance threshold, and PTT-specific return-to-running criteria are not established.
policies.evidence_certainty: Low for PTT treatment thresholds; high for avoiding diagnostic overreach
policies.threshold_basis: Clinical-safety principle; no numeric pain cutoff
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate tolerated activity only from repeated athlete responses and clinician input.
policies.uncertainty: The app cannot distinguish tendinopathy, dysfunction/PCFD, or another cause of medial ankle pain.
review_triggers: Swelling, weakness, deformity concern, or loss of function appears
Symptoms fail to settle between exposures

policies.title: Use delayed tendon response before progression
policies.decision_question: Did the previous run demonstrate tolerance sufficient to progress?
trigger: A run—especially a long or novel run—was followed by symptoms later the same day or over a later follow-up window, or the delayed response is unknown.
suggested_action: Link the delayed response to the provoking session in the audit trail.
Hold or reduce the next comparable mechanical exposure until the response is understood rather than progressing automatically.
Progress only one primary load dimension after a repeatable, acceptable response.
alternatives: Keep an easy shorter run if daily function and symptoms are stable within the athlete’s established tolerance
Substitute low-impact aerobic work
Retain nonprovocative strength work
do_not_apply_when: A clinician has provided different monitoring criteria.
Acute trauma or red-flag symptoms require assessment rather than routine load management.
policies.rationale: PTT trials do not validate a return-to-run cutoff; Achilles pain-monitoring evidence supports the concept of tracked response but its numbers do not transfer.
policies.evidence_certainty: Low for PTT-specific criteria; moderate for single-session association
policies.threshold_basis: Athlete-calibrated symptom/function trend; all imported tendon numeric cutoffs remain null
policies.calibration_needed: Define an acceptable response with a clinician or repeated athlete-specific observations; store delayed checks as timestamped observations.
policies.uncertainty: Attribution is imperfect when running, lifting, footwear, and daily activity cluster.
review_triggers: The same load produces progressively worse response

policies.title: Progress one primary running-load dimension
policies.decision_question: How should running load advance during a tendon-limited rebuild?
trigger: The recent cycle was completed with stable symptoms, acceptable recovery, and no illness, and the next cycle is being proposed.
suggested_action: Preserve the currently agreed run frequency unless the user changes it.
Choose one primary progression target—such as easy-run duration, long-run duration, or quality dose—while keeping the others broadly stable.
Use a consolidation cycle when tolerance is uncertain rather than forcing a fixed increase.
alternatives: Repeat the prior cycle
Redistribute duration across easy runs without increasing total
Use cross-training for additional aerobic work without claiming one-for-one running load
do_not_apply_when: The previous cycle was not tolerated, illness is active/recent, or the athlete is adding a new high-impact stimulus.
policies.rationale: No universal safe percentage is supported; simultaneous changes make cause and tolerance harder to interpret.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for rejecting a universal rule; low for exact progression
policies.threshold_basis: Coaching heuristic grounded in uncertainty and observability; numeric increase null
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate the size and duration of each progression from repeated 14-day tolerance and goals.
policies.uncertainty: Holding other variables stable is not always possible; life stress and strength work remain confounders.
review_triggers: A new surface, hill, shoe, speed, or plyometric stimulus is introduced

policies.title: Flag novel single-run load without declaring a safe boundary
policies.decision_question: Should a run longer than recent history be modified?
trigger: The planned run is materially longer than the recent longest comparable run or falls into a dashboard-defined novelty band.
suggested_action: Surface the novelty explicitly and offer a shorter, flatter, easier, or split alternative.
Treat any percentage as an observational flag, not a clearance line.
Require delayed-response follow-up before using the new distance as the next baseline.
alternatives: Repeat the recent longest tolerated run
Add low-impact aerobic time after a shorter run
Move some duration to another easy run in the cycle without increasing frequency
do_not_apply_when: Recent history is incomplete or includes noncomparable terrain/intensity; label the comparison unreliable.
policies.rationale: A large Garmin cohort associated single-session distance spikes with injury, but observational cut points do not establish causality or a PTT-specific threshold.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for association; low for causal cutoff
policies.athlete_applicability: High as a warning, not as a gate
policies.threshold_basis: Study-derived association used as a descriptive flag; exact dashboard bands require calibration
policies.calibration_needed: Choose lookback and comparison logic with enough data; consider duration as well as distance for hills or heat.
policies.uncertainty: The cohort outcome and distance categories may not match this athlete or tendon.
review_triggers: The novel run also adds pace, hills, or surface change

policies.title: Limit demanding exposure during the rebuild
policies.decision_question: Does the current two-week plan contain too much demanding load?
trigger: A proposed 14-day segment contains quality work, a mechanically substantial long run, hard strength sessions, hills/strides/plyometrics, or other demanding exposures close together.
suggested_action: Count demanding exposures by physiological and mechanical demand, not labels alone.
During the tendon-limited rebuild, keep one formal quality run and one long run per week only when the long run remains controlled and both are tolerated; otherwise modify one exposure.
Do not add a second formal quality day merely to satisfy a distribution model.
alternatives: Make the long run shorter/easier
Replace the quality session with controlled strides only after tolerance is established
Use an easy aerobic or low-impact session
do_not_apply_when: The athlete’s phase, diagnosis, and tolerance have changed and a revised plan has been agreed.
policies.rationale: No intensity distribution is universally superior, and a long run can be demanding despite low intensity. Low run frequency makes session-count ratios especially misleading.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for distribution uncertainty; insufficient for a universal exposure cap
policies.threshold_basis: Phase-specific coaching heuristic; no fixed count beyond preserving the current agreed pattern
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate what counts as demanding using RPE, duration, terrain, symptoms, and strength proximity.
policies.uncertainty: The same session can have different cost as fitness and tendon tolerance change.

policies.title: Do not classify a fast long run from pace alone
policies.decision_question: Was a long run easy, steady, or demanding?
trigger: A long-run pace appears fast relative to recent race performance, but effort, terrain, weather, heart-rate quality, and RPE are missing or uncertain.
suggested_action: Label effort classification unknown rather than calling the pace easy or hard.
Use it as a completed mechanical exposure and request the smallest missing context needed for future classification.
Avoid using it to reset easy-pace targets or justify progression.
alternatives: Compare later against a standardized route/conditions
Use RPE and talk-test next time
Treat it conservatively in weekly load review
do_not_apply_when: Reliable RPE, HR, route, and conditions already establish the intended and actual effort.
policies.rationale: Pace/HR and decoupling are condition-dependent; a single pace cannot define intensity.
policies.athlete_applicability: Very high for the known reported long run
policies.calibration_needed: Build athlete-specific comparisons from repeated, comparable runs.
policies.uncertainty: RPE is also imperfect and HR can be affected by heat, hills, illness, caffeine, and sensor error.
review_triggers: Repeated mismatch between pace, HR, and RPE

policies.title: Schedule strength as a coequal goal
policies.decision_question: How should twice-weekly full-body strength coexist with quality and long running?
trigger: A run or lifting session must be placed or moved within the 14-day cycle.
suggested_action: Preserve two meaningful full-body strength sessions unless the user changes that goal.
Avoid placing unfamiliar, high-soreness lower-body work immediately before a key run.
When same-day consolidation is useful, separate sessions when practical and order the higher-priority adaptation first; do not assume one universal order.
alternatives: Preferred strength days with key runs arranged around observed soreness
alternate strength days rotation when it better separates demanding lower-body work
Same-day easy run plus strength to preserve recovery days
do_not_apply_when: Acute injury, clinician restriction, or a short race-specific taper temporarily changes priorities.
policies.rationale: Concurrent training generally preserves maximal strength and hypertrophy, while explosive outcomes and same-session interference require more care.
policies.threshold_basis: Evidence-informed scheduling principle; no universal separation-hour rule
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate around actual soreness, exercise selection, and which goal is prioritized in the current phase.
policies.uncertainty: Meta-analyses do not identify one best weekly arrangement for this athlete.
review_triggers: Persistent interference with run quality or strength progression
PTT loading from calf work or plyometrics increases

policies.title: Modify for interfering strength soreness
policies.decision_question: What should happen when lower-body soreness is near a quality or long run?
trigger: Lower-body soreness, stiffness, or fatigue from strength training is likely to alter gait, coordination, or target quality.
suggested_action: Use warm-up movement and easy running to determine whether the planned quality is intact.
If mechanics or effort are meaningfully altered, convert the run to easy, shorten it, or reschedule without adding an extra session.
Review strength placement, volume, novelty, and proximity to failure.
alternatives: Low-impact aerobic work
Upper-body/emphasis-adjusted lifting
Keep the run easy and retain the next planned recovery day
do_not_apply_when: Soreness is focal, sharp, worsening, associated with swelling/weakness, or indistinguishable from injury; use symptom/clinical policies.
policies.rationale: The practical issue is not soreness itself but whether it degrades the higher-priority session or compounds mechanical load.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for concurrent-training interaction; heuristic for daily choice
policies.threshold_basis: Athlete-calibrated functional heuristic; no numeric soreness cutoff
policies.calibration_needed: Record which exercises and doses reliably produce interfering soreness.
policies.uncertainty: DOMS and injury are not reliably distinguished by a score alone.

policies.title: Do not make up missed sessions
policies.decision_question: Should missed runs or lifts be compressed into the remaining days?
trigger: One or more planned sessions were missed because of illness, schedule, fatigue, or symptoms.
suggested_action: Resume from the current state rather than compressing all missed work.
Keep the agreed frequency and prioritize continuity: easy/base work, then one key stimulus if tolerated.
Treat the miss as lost training, not debt.
alternatives: Drop optional volume
Move one key session while preserving recovery
Repeat a prior tolerated cycle segment
do_not_apply_when: A coach/user has intentionally rescheduled a single session with adequate recovery and no load compression.
policies.rationale: Illness return is staged, and single-session novelty may matter more than satisfying a planned weekly total.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate clinical/observational support; strong coaching rationale
policies.threshold_basis: Coaching convention supported by load-management logic; no numeric rule
policies.calibration_needed: Learn which sessions are highest priority for the current phase.
policies.uncertainty: There is little direct trial evidence comparing make-up strategies.
review_triggers: Multiple misses suggest the plan is unrealistic
Compression would place demanding exposures back-to-back

policies.title: Avoid simultaneous volume and intensity escalation
policies.decision_question: Should the next cycle increase both running volume and workout intensity?
trigger: The proposed segment increases total running, longest run, and/or intensity dose at the same time, especially with new hills, strides, plyometrics, or strength loading.
suggested_action: Choose the primary adaptation target and hold the other major variables broadly stable.
When both changes are unavoidable, reduce their magnitude, mark the cycle as a higher-uncertainty trial, and add delayed-response review.
alternatives: Increase easy duration while maintaining quality dose
Progress quality while consolidating total and long-run duration
Progress strength while holding running load
do_not_apply_when: A supervised plan deliberately uses a combined change and the athlete has demonstrated tolerance.
policies.rationale: No universal safe progression exists; changing multiple stimuli simultaneously reduces attribution and may increase cumulative cost.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for uncertainty; heuristic for attribution
policies.threshold_basis: Coaching heuristic; no numeric combined-load threshold
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate by phase and repeated response.
policies.uncertainty: Some training adaptations require mixed stimuli; this policy manages uncertainty rather than claiming causation.
review_triggers: New stimulus proves more costly than expected

policies.title: Control environmental and sensor confounding
policies.decision_question: Is a dashboard trend real enough to change training?
trigger: Pace, heart rate, decoupling, sleep, HRV, VO2max, or readiness changes materially, but weather, hills, surface, device fit, firmware, or signal quality also changed.
suggested_action: Do not interpret the metric as fitness loss or readiness failure until comparable observations accumulate.
Annotate confounders and use standardized comparisons where possible.
Prefer symptoms, RPE, and repeat observations over a single noisy value.
alternatives: Use duration/RPE instead of pace in heat or hills
Exclude implausible HR segments
Use a chest strap for interval precision if the athlete chooses
do_not_apply_when: A clinically concerning symptom is present; do not dismiss it as sensor error.
policies.rationale: Wearable and pace/HR measures have condition-specific error; proprietary composites add no validated coaching cutoff.
policies.evidence_certainty: Low-moderate for device-specific validity; high for confounding principle
policies.threshold_basis: Measurement-quality rule; thresholds device- and athlete-specific
policies.calibration_needed: Define comparable-route tags and automated plausibility checks after inspecting the actual export.
policies.uncertainty: A real physiological change and a measurement artifact can coexist.

policies.title: Use cross-training as support, not a running equivalent
policies.decision_question: Should aerobic work be shifted to cycling or another low-impact mode?
trigger: Running load is constrained by PTT symptoms, illness return, schedule, or mechanical tolerance while general aerobic work remains appropriate.
suggested_action: Use a tolerated low-impact mode to preserve or add aerobic stimulus without claiming it replaces running durability one-for-one.
Start from mode-specific effort/duration experience and monitor symptoms.
Keep some tolerated running exposure when appropriate so running-specific tissue adaptation is not assumed to transfer.
alternatives: Rest
Shorter run plus low-impact work
Pool running/elliptical/cycling selected by symptom response and access
do_not_apply_when: The mode provokes symptoms, illness guidance calls for rest, or the athlete lacks safe familiarity/equipment.
policies.rationale: Small trials and a recent meta-analysis support some aerobic maintenance, but transfer and optimal substitution ratios are uncertain.
policies.athlete_applicability: High when running is mechanically constrained
policies.calibration_needed: Learn RPE/HR response and recovery for each mode.
policies.uncertainty: Evidence is short-term and heterogeneous; tissue loading differs.
review_triggers: Running-specific fitness declines despite maintained aerobic metrics

policies.title: Check fueling before labeling fatigue as overtraining
policies.decision_question: Could inadequate fueling contribute to poor recovery or a weak session?
trigger: Fatigue, poor recovery, declining performance, irritability, or repeated low-energy sessions occur, particularly around quality, long runs, or combined run-lift days.
suggested_action: Ask a brief, nonjudgmental preparedness question rather than infer nutrition status.
Encourage carbohydrate availability around demanding/long sessions and regular protein-containing meals using flexible food-based options.
Do not diagnose REDs or prescribe calorie tracking from Garmin estimates.
alternatives: Simplify the session
Move demanding work until adequately prepared
Refer to a sports dietitian/clinician when persistent concerns or health signs exist
do_not_apply_when: The athlete has clinician-directed nutrition care that should govern the decision.
The fatigue is explained by acute illness or another urgent condition; address that first.
policies.rationale: Energy availability is clinically multifactorial; carbohydrate supports higher-demand work and protein supports resistance adaptation, but exact needs are individual.
policies.evidence_certainty: Moderate for general principles; low for individual diagnosis
policies.athlete_applicability: High for hybrid training; low for diagnosing status
policies.threshold_basis: Consensus/position-statement guidance; individual gram/calorie thresholds null unless user/clinician supplies them
policies.calibration_needed: Calibrate simple prompts to session duration, GI tolerance, preferences, and goals.
policies.uncertainty: The dashboard cannot infer intake, absorption, energy availability, or REDs from wearable expenditure.
review_triggers: Menstrual/endocrine, bone, weight, or eating concerns if disclosed

policies.title: Escalate when self-directed load adjustment is insufficient
policies.decision_question: When should the coach stop optimizing and recommend clinical input?
trigger: Symptoms are progressive, recurrent, function-limiting, diagnostically unclear, or not settling with reasonable load modification; or a red flag appears.
suggested_action: State that the app cannot diagnose the condition.
Recommend assessment by an appropriate clinician while avoiding an invented diagnosis or rehab protocol.
Until assessed, avoid repeatedly testing the same provoking exposure and preserve only clearly tolerated activity.
alternatives: Use nonprovocative training
Document symptom timeline and training context for the clinician
Pause impact loading when function is deteriorating
do_not_apply_when: Minor, clearly improving soreness with normal function and a known benign cause may be monitored; still use uncertainty language.
policies.rationale: PTT symptoms span conditions from local tendinopathy to dysfunction/PCFD and other diagnoses; trials do not supply a universal self-management boundary.
policies.evidence_certainty: High for diagnostic boundary; low for exact escalation timing
policies.calibration_needed: A clinician may define individualized pain/function criteria and loading.
policies.uncertainty: The package cannot list every red flag or replace examination.
review_triggers: New weakness, swelling, shape change, or acute trauma
